item.title: Claude Code's Built-In Plan and Explore Subagents Run Without Any Setup — They're Read-Only Sandboxes for Codebase Exploration That Can't Accidentally Write a File
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: Plan and Explore are built-in Claude Code subagents that need no .claude/agents/ definition — they search and analyze your codebase read-only and cannot write, delete, or run shell commands.
item.content:encoded:
**Plan and Explore are built-in Claude Code subagents that run without any `.claude/agents/` setup — both are read-only sandboxes that can search and analyze your codebase but cannot write, delete, or execute shell commands.**
When you trigger `/plan` or ask Claude to plan a change, it doesn't do all the file reading in your main session — it delegates that phase to the built-in **Plan** agent. Plan runs with a restricted tool set: Read, Glob, Grep, and nothing else. No Bash, no Edit. The exploration stays isolated from your main context window, and none of it can accidentally modify anything.
**Explore** is the same idea for on-demand research. Invoke it for any multi-file search task where you want sandboxed exploration without polluting the main session. Because it's read-only, you can run it alongside an implementation session — Explore researches in parallel, finds what you need, and returns a summary; the main session writes files. Neither runs in the other's context.
**What you'll be able to do after this:** - Understand why `/plan` keeps exploration isolated from your main context — and what that means for plan quality on a messy codebase - Explicitly invoke the Explore agent for multi-file audits or codebase surveys you don't want eating your main context - Trust the safety property: neither Plan nor Explore can write, delete, or run shell commands
**The key difference from custom `.claude/agents/` subagents:** You don't define a file for Plan or Explore. Claude Code ships them and picks them automatically. You can override the defaults (including the model they use) by creating a `.claude/agents/explore.md` file — but out of the box they require no configuration.
**When NOT to use them:** The subagent overhead isn't worth it for a targeted grep or a single-file lookup. Plan and Explore earn their keep when the exploration spans many files and would otherwise leave dozens of file-read results in the main session's context. For anything simpler, stay in the main session.
A practical limit: if you've split your project across many directories without cross-linked CLAUDE.md files, Explore may miss relevant context that a manual search would catch. The agent reads what it can access from the project root; it doesn't load directory-specific CLAUDE.md files outside of the paths it visits.
**Sources:** [Claude Code sub-agents — official docs](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sub-agents), [How and when to use subagents in Claude Code](https://claude.com/blog/how-and-when-to-use-subagents-in-claude-code), [Practical guide: Claude Code subagents 2026](https://tembo.io/blog/claude-code-subagents), [3 patterns for saving context with subagents](https://vantaige.io/blog/claude-code-subagents-save-context-3-patterns)

item.title: Your Claude Design Canvas Doesn't Know What You Built Last Sprint — Run /design-sync in Claude Code to Push Your Repo Components Into the Canvas So Explorations Stay on Your Real Code
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: Run /design-sync from Claude Code to push your component library into Claude Design; the canvas then explores changes on your real components instead of generating generic defaults.
item.content:encoded:
**Run `/design-sync` in Claude Code to push your actual component library into Claude Design — the canvas then explores changes on your real Button, Card, and Form components instead of generating generic defaults that don't match your codebase.**
When you open Claude Design after a sprint of building in Claude Code, the canvas doesn't know what you actually shipped. It generates a Button that uses the wrong variant API, applies spacing that doesn't match your tokens, and produces components you'd rewrite from scratch before dropping into the repo. This is the reverse-direction problem: the Claude Design → Claude Code handoff exists, but the other way — bringing your real code back into the canvas — requires a deliberate sync.
**What you'll be able to do after this:** - Explore UI changes in Claude Design on your actual component set, not generic approximations - Round-trip cleanly: design → export → build in Claude Code → `/design-sync` back — each direction feeds the other without drift - Understand what gets lost in each direction so you can anticipate where to verify after a sync
**Steps:** 1. In Claude Code, run `/design-sync` from your project root. 2. Review the plan Claude proposes — a list of each component Claude Design will learn about, plus files to write or delete in the Claude Design workspace. 3. Approve; the sync runs incrementally, one component at a time. 4. Open Claude Design: explorations now start from your real component tree.
**Limits:** The first sync can take a while on a large repo — one account of a medium-sized design system reported roughly 40 minutes. The sync is a snapshot, not a live watch; re-run it after significant refactors or renames. Independent testing at [gaugr.app](https://gaugr.app/en/blog/claude-design-2-update-design-systems-code-sync-guide) found framework coverage gaps: complex component trees with heavy prop drilling or deeply nested compound components may produce approximate representations. Verify critical components in the Claude Design workspace after the sync, rather than assuming the canvas matches the repo exactly.
The sync doesn't give Claude Design access to your component's runtime behavior — it captures structure, props, and styling. Logic that's only visible at runtime (animation states, async data shapes) won't appear in the canvas.
**Sources:** [Get started with Claude Design](https://support.claude.com/en/articles/14604416-get-started-with-claude-design), [Claude Design two-way sync blog post](https://claude.com/blog/claude-design-stays-on-brand-for-daily-work), [design-sync guide with limits — gaugr.app](https://gaugr.app/en/blog/claude-design-2-update-design-systems-code-sync-guide), [How to sync a design system with Claude Design — nitayneeman.com](https://nitayneeman.com/blog/how-to-sync-a-design-system-with-claude-design/)

item.title: Your Shell Script Has No Way to Call Claude Code — `claude -p` Runs One Prompt Non-Interactively, Reads Stdin, and Writes the Response to Stdout for CI and Batch Jobs
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: The --print / -p flag runs Claude Code non-interactively — one prompt in, one response out, no session, no approval prompts — making it a scriptable AI step in CI pipelines and shell scripts.
item.content:encoded:
**`claude -p "prompt"` makes Claude Code non-interactive — one prompt in, response to stdout, no session, no approval prompts — so it works as a pipe stage in any shell script or CI job.**
The `--print` flag (or `-p`) switches Claude Code out of the interactive REPL. It reads stdin if you pipe to it, runs the prompt once, writes the response to stdout, and exits. You can capture the output like any other command:
```bash # Summarize a PR diff for the description git diff main...HEAD | claude -p "Write a concise PR description for these changes."
# Surface the root cause from a failing test run pnpm test 2>&1 | tail -200 | claude -p "What caused this test failure? Show the root cause and a one-line fix."
# Review a file before committing claude -p "Flag any security issues in this file:" < src/api/auth.ts
# Capture output for further shell processing SUMMARY=$(git log --oneline -20 | claude -p "Summarize the theme of these commits in one sentence.") echo "Theme: $SUMMARY" ```
**What breaks in this mode:** `-p` does not load your project's CLAUDE.md context or `.claude/settings.json` tool restrictions, so the model has no knowledge of your project conventions — put relevant constraints directly in the prompt. Sessions are ephemeral (no `/resume`, no history). No tool calls or file writes happen; output is text only.
**Rate limits in batch loops:** if you're running `-p` across dozens of files in a `for` loop, space the calls out (`sleep 2`) or switch to `--model haiku` for speed-insensitive jobs.
**Sources:** [Claude Code CLI reference — code.claude.com](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/cli-reference) · [Non-interactive usage patterns — docs.claude.com](https://docs.claude.com/en/claude-code/cli-usage) · [Simon Willison's `llm` CLI: the same Unix-pipeline idea for arbitrary models](https://llm.datasette.io/en/stable/usage.html)

item.title: GitHub Copilot's Code Scanning Agent Explores the Codebase, Proposes a Fix, Re-runs CodeQL, and Opens a PR — Enterprise Advanced Security Only, Billed per Agent Session
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: GitHub Copilot's agentic autofix for code scanning is GA: assign a CodeQL alert and an agent explores files, writes a fix, verifies it, and opens a PR. Enterprise Advanced Security only.
item.content:encoded:
**GitHub Copilot's agentic autofix for code scanning is GA: assign a CodeQL alert to Copilot, and an agent explores affected files, drafts a fix, re-runs the standard query suite to verify it, and opens a pull request — up to 25 alerts per session.**
The workflow lives entirely in GitHub: an admin enables the "agentic autofix" policy, then any developer can assign a default-branch alert to Copilot from the code scanning alert view. The agent iterates on the fix until verification passes (or reports it couldn't), then opens the PR for review.
Constraints not foregrounded in the announcement: this requires GitHub Enterprise Cloud with Code Security or Advanced Security — no Standard plan. Billing adds Copilot cloud agent sessions on top of whatever GitHub Actions the verification run consumes. Only the standard CodeQL query suite is used for the verification pass; custom queries don't run, so a fix that breaks a custom rule won't be caught before the PR opens. Fix quality has not yet been independently benchmarked outside GitHub's own reporting.
**Why it matters:** The "scanning found 847 alerts, nobody has touched them in six months" problem has a mechanized path to a PR for the first time in a mainstream workflow. Whether the fix PR is merge-ready still needs review — but the gap between "alert exists" and "there's a PR to look at" is now closeable.
**Sources:** [GitHub Changelog — Agentic Autofix for Code Scanning GA, Oct 15](https://github.blog/changelog/2026-10-15-agentic-autofix-for-code-scanning-alerts-general-availability) · [GitHub Advanced Security billing for agent sessions — docs.github.com](https://docs.github.com/en/billing/managing-billing-for-github-advanced-security/about-billing-for-github-advanced-security)

item.title: A Full Fine-Tune of an 8B Model Needs 64+ GB of VRAM — QLoRA With Unsloth Runs the Same Model in 4-Bit on a Free Colab T4, Cutting Peak VRAM to Under 10 GB
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: QLoRA quantizes the frozen base model to 4-bit, so Llama 3.1 8B fine-tunes in under 10 GB of VRAM on a free Colab T4. Unsloth's notebook is the fastest way to run it.
item.content:encoded:
**QLoRA quantizes the frozen base model to 4-bit so only the small LoRA adapter weights train in full precision — Llama 3.1 8B fits in under 10 GB of VRAM, which a free Colab T4 has.**
**What you'll be able to do after this:** - Fine-tune a Llama 3.1 8B instruction model on your own dataset using a free GPU - Understand what QLoRA does differently from standard LoRA (and why the VRAM number is so much lower) - Export the result as a GGUF file to load locally with Ollama, or push the adapter weights to HuggingFace Hub
**Why the VRAM drops:** standard LoRA keeps the base model in bf16 (~16 GB for 8B parameters). QLoRA quantizes the frozen base to NF4 (a 4-bit normal float format from the [Dettmers et al. QLoRA paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.14314)), reducing it to ~4 GB. The LoRA adapters — the only weights actually updated during training — stay in bf16. Unsloth reports peak VRAM around 6–10 GB for Llama 3.1 8B (vendor-reported; varies by batch size and sequence length).
**Steps** — open the [Unsloth Llama 3.1 fine-tuning notebook](https://unsloth.ai/docs/get-started/fine-tuning-llms-guide) (one-click Colab link on that page):
1. **Runtime → Change runtime type → T4 GPU** in Colab (free tier). 2. **Install:** `pip install unsloth` 3. **Load the base model in 4-bit:** ```python from unsloth import FastLanguageModel model, tokenizer = FastLanguageModel.from_pretrained( model_name="unsloth/Meta-Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct", max_seq_length=2048, load_in_4bit=True, # activates QLoRA — base weights stored as NF4 ) ``` 4. **Attach LoRA adapters** (only these train): ```python model = FastLanguageModel.get_peft_model( model, r=16, lora_alpha=16, target_modules=["q_proj","k_proj","v_proj","o_proj", "gate_proj","up_proj","down_proj"], ) ``` 5. **Train on your Alpaca-format dataset** — use the recipe from the [Oct 9 dataset post](/ai-news/2026-10-09-07-alpaca-jsonl-instruction-tuning-dataset-lima-quality). 6. **Export:** ```python # GGUF for Ollama model.save_pretrained_gguf("model_gguf", tokenizer, quantization_method="q4_k_m") # or push adapters to HuggingFace Hub model.push_to_hub("your-username/my-llama-adapter", token="HF_TOKEN") ```
**Limits:** The free T4's 15 GB caps you at roughly 12B-parameter models with QLoRA — larger models need Colab Pro (A100/L4) or a local 24 GB+ card. Unsloth's speed and memory figures are vendor-reported; independently measured results vary by architecture and sequence length. And 4-bit base weights do degrade output quality slightly compared to full bf16 fine-tuning — QLoRA is a memory–quality trade-off, not a free lunch.
**Sources:** [Unsloth fine-tuning guide with one-click Colab notebooks — unsloth.ai](https://unsloth.ai/docs/get-started/fine-tuning-llms-guide) · [QLoRA: Efficient Finetuning of Quantized LLMs — arXiv:2305.14314](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.14314) · [Fine-tuning with Unsloth QLoRA walkthrough — computingforgeeks.com](https://computingforgeeks.com/fine-tune-llm-unsloth-qlora/)

item.title: Claude Code Truncates Your Test Output Before the Failing Assertion — `bashOutputMaxChars` and `taskOutputMaxChars` in settings.json Raise the Cap to 128K
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: Two settings.json keys raise Claude Code's Bash and task output cap to 128K characters so test failures and compile errors stop getting cut before you reach them.
item.content:encoded:
**Two settings.json keys let you raise Claude Code's Bash and task output cap to 128,000 characters — the failing assertion stops getting cut from the bottom of your test run.**
When a verbose test runner, a TypeScript type check, or a large `git diff` runs inside a Claude Code session, the raw output is silently cut at the tool's inline display limit — the error or failure is usually near the end, which is exactly where it gets truncated.
Two settings added in v2.1.263 control this. Add them to `.claude/settings.json` (project-scoped) or `~/.claude/settings.json` (global):
```json { "bashOutputMaxChars": 128000, "taskOutputMaxChars": 128000 } ```
- **`bashOutputMaxChars`** — caps Bash tool inline output. Raise this when `jest --verbose`, `pytest -s -v`, or `tsc --noEmit` gets cut before the assertion you need. - **`taskOutputMaxChars`** — caps output from background subagent tasks. Raise this when you've delegated a CI-style run to a subagent and need the full log to diagnose failures after the fact.
**When to set globally vs. per-project:** if you only need verbose output for one project's test suite, set it in that project's `.claude/settings.json`. If you routinely work with verbose tooling across projects, set it in `~/.claude/settings.json`.
**Limit:** longer inline output means more tokens in context per tool call. On a tight context budget, or when you run many Bash calls in sequence, the context window fills faster. Pair this setting with explicit `allowedTools` restrictions to avoid tools that produce verbose noise you won't act on.
**Sources:** [Claude Code v2.1.263 release summary — claudelog.com](https://www.claudelog.com/claude-code-changelog/) · [Claude Code context window and compaction — morphllm.com](https://www.morphllm.com/claude-code-context-window)

item.title: Your Vector Store Returns Documents About RAG Instead of Documents Mentioning "RAG v0.9" — Hybrid BM25 Plus Dense Search Fuses Both Rankings With RRF in Qdrant
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: Dense search encodes meaning but blurs exact tokens; BM25 catches them by term frequency; Qdrant's native hybrid mode fuses both rankings server-side via RRF.
item.content:encoded:
**Dense search encodes meaning but blurs exact tokens; BM25 catches them by term frequency; running both and fusing via RRF consistently outperforms either alone on mixed-query RAG workloads.**
**What you'll be able to do after this:** build a hybrid BM25 + dense retrieval pipeline that finds documents by meaning *and* by exact keyword — so searches for version strings, error codes, API identifiers, and technical terms don't disappear into the embedding space.
- Dense embeddings encode semantic similarity but smear exact tokens. Searching "LangChain v0.3 deprecation" produces a vector near "LangChain framework changes" — useful, but it may miss a document that literally contains the string "v0.3". - BM25 scores by token frequency weighted by inverse document frequency (IDF) — it finds exact term matches that dense search misses. - Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF) merges two ranked lists by position rather than by raw score, so BM25 term counts and cosine similarity values (on different numeric scales) combine without normalization.
**Walk-through (Qdrant, self-hosted or cloud):**
```bash pip install qdrant-client fastembed ```
Create a collection with a dense vector and a BM25 sparse vector:
```python from qdrant_client import QdrantClient, models
client = QdrantClient(url="http://localhost:6333") # or ":memory:"
client.create_collection( "docs", vectors_config={"dense": models.VectorParams(size=384, distance=models.Distance.COSINE)}, sparse_vectors_config={ "bm25": models.SparseVectorParams(modifier=models.Modifier.IDF) }, ) ```
At query time, pass two `prefetch` sub-queries and fuse with `FusionQuery`:
```python results = client.query_points( collection_name="docs", prefetch=[ models.Prefetch(query=dense_vec, using="dense", limit=20), models.Prefetch(query=sparse_vec, using="bm25", limit=20), ], query=models.FusionQuery(fusion=models.Fusion.RRF), limit=5, ) ```
Qdrant computes the RRF fusion server-side — no manual rank-combination code needed. With Qdrant Cloud Inference you can pass a plain text string as `query` and skip the local embedding model entirely.
**Limits:** sparse vectors add ~20–30% storage overhead. BM25 IDF is computed at index time across the full corpus — adding documents later recomputes IDF, which can shift rankings for existing queries. For very short queries (one or two tokens), BM25 can dominate over semantics; reduce the RRF k-constant below 60 to soften that effect.
**Sources:** [Qdrant Hybrid Search with Reranking — qdrant.tech](https://qdrant.tech/documentation/tutorials-basics/reranking-hybrid-search/) · [Hybrid BM25 + Vector + RRF 2026 reference — sidhya.studio](https://sidhya.studio/posts/hybrid-bm25-vector-rerank-2026-reference) · [Hybrid Search with LangChain — LanceDB blog](https://lancedb.substack.com/p/hybrid-search-combining-bm25-and)

item.title: Your PR Review Queue Is the Bottleneck, Not Your Inference Speed — Harvard Finds AI Coding Agents Raise Code Output +30% With No Gain in Shipped Features
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: A Harvard working paper on 700+ software firms found AI coding agents raised code output 30% with no gain in resolved issues; PR merge times rose 49%.
item.content:encoded:
**A Harvard working paper finds AI coding agents raised per-worker code output ~30% across 700+ firms — but resolved issues were flat, PR merge time rose 49%, and revision requests nearly doubled; the bottleneck is review, not generation.**
Fiona Chen and James Stratton (Harvard, "Artificial Intelligence in the Firm," Aug 2026) used Jellyfish engineering analytics data from over 700 software companies between 2021–2026. Workers using AI coding agents produced roughly 1,500 extra lines per month (+30%), 20% more commits, and 23% more pull requests. Resolved Jira issues and completed epics showed no statistically significant change; firm-level headcount held flat.
The identified constraint: review. PR-to-merge time rose 49%. Revision requests nearly doubled. The share of workers assigned to review grew 14%.
Practical read: adding generation capacity without matching review bandwidth shifts the queue, not the throughput. If your team is already reviewer-limited, more AI-generated PRs accelerate that constraint rather than relieving it.
One caveat: the study measures commit and PR metadata, not shipped-feature quality or post-merge impact. It covers adoption through early 2026, and both the tools and the workflow patterns around them continue to change.
**Also this week:** NVIDIA released [Nemotron 3.5 Bolt 74B](https://www.techrepublic.com/article/news-nvidia-nemotron-3-5-super-vl-bolt-ai-models/) — an open model (24 GB VRAM, ~9B active parameters per NVIDIA's own figures) built for local agentic workloads — available now on Ollama, LM Studio, and llama.cpp. OpenRouter's earlier testing of the Nemotron 3.5 Lightning variant found lower accuracy than NVIDIA's benchmarks, so measure on your own tasks.
**Why it matters:** The Harvard finding reframes where AI coding tool ROI actually lands — invest in review tooling and process, not just a faster model.
**Sources:** [Harvard: AI Coding Agents Lift Code 30%, Shipped Output Flat — aiweekly.co](https://aiweekly.co/alerts/harvard-study-ai-coding-agents-lift-code-30-shipped-output-flat) · [Byteiota coverage and analysis](https://byteiota.com/ai-coding-agents-write-30-more-code-teams-ship-the-same/) · [NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Bolt — TechRepublic](https://www.techrepublic.com/article/news-nvidia-nemotron-3-5-super-vl-bolt-ai-models/) · [HPC Wire on Nemotron 3.5](https://www.hpcwire.com/aiwire/2026/10/15/nvidia-expands-nemotron-family-with-highest-efficiency-super-vl-and-bolt-models/)

item.title: Your Chunks Lose the Context That Made Them Retrievable — Late Chunking Embeds the Full Document First, Then Splits
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: Late chunking embeds the full document first, then splits the resulting token embeddings per chunk — so each chunk inherits its surrounding document context.
item.content:encoded:
**Late chunking embeds the full document first, then splits the resulting token embeddings at chunk boundaries — each chunk inherits its surrounding document context, not just its own text.**
**What you'll be able to do after this:** generate chunk embeddings that capture cross-chunk references, so pronouns and entity mentions in a chunk don't become dead ends in your vector index.
Standard RAG: split text → embed each chunk in isolation. The problem: "It increased 40% in Q3" produces a semantically vague embedding because the model only sees that sentence. Your vector store indexes it faithfully, but no plausible query can retrieve it reliably.
Late chunking flips the order:
1. Run the **full document** through a long-context embedding model to get one embedding **per token**. 2. Split at your chunk boundaries and **average** the token embeddings for each span.
Each chunk embedding is conditioned on its full document context. Cross-references, pronouns, and topic continuity survive the split.
**With the Jina API (hosted, one call):**
```python import requests, os
response = requests.post( "https://api.jina.ai/v1/embeddings", headers={"Authorization": f"Bearer {os.environ['JINA_API_KEY']}"}, json={ "model": "jina-embeddings-v3", "late_chunking": True, "input": [ full_document, # index 0 — discard this embedding chunk_1, chunk_2, chunk_3, ] } ) chunk_embeddings = [d["embedding"] for d in response.json()["data"][1:]] ```
Send the full document as the first element and your chunks after it. Discard `data[0]`; store the rest in your vector store as usual.
**Limit:** Late chunking helps most when chunks have cross-document dependencies — financial reports, technical documentation, meeting notes. For self-contained paragraphs (e.g. FAQ entries), the gain over standard chunking is marginal. `jina-embeddings-v3` has an 8,192-token context window; documents longer than that need a sliding-window approach or a different long-context model.
**Sources:** [Late Chunking in Long-Context Embedding Models — jina.ai](https://jina.ai/news/late-chunking-in-long-context-embedding-models/) · [Late Chunking hands-on tutorial — DataCamp](https://www.datacamp.com/tutorial/late-chunking) · [Hosted API implementation guide — TDS course](https://tds.s-anand.net/2026-02/docs/week-4/late-chunking/)

item.title: Your Auto Mode Logs Don't Tell You Why a Tool Was Blocked — v2.1.301 Adds classifier_verdict and permission_mode to Every tool_decision Span
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: Claude Code v2.1.301 adds classifier_verdict and permission_mode to tool_decision OTel spans — traces now show whether auto mode's classifier or a permission rule blocked each tool call.
item.content:encoded:
**Claude Code v2.1.301 adds `classifier_verdict` and `permission_mode` to `claude_code.tool_decision` spans — your OTel backend can now distinguish classifier blocks from permission-rule blocks in unattended runs.**
Auto mode logs a `claude_code.tool_decision` event on every tool call decision. Before v2.1.301, the event carried `tool_name`, `decision`, and `source`, but nothing that distinguished why a call was blocked: you couldn't tell whether auto mode's classifier refused it or a permission rule in your `settings.json` denied it. Both showed up as "blocked", pointing you at the wrong part of your configuration when you tried to debug.
**What v2.1.301 adds (October 15):** - `classifier_verdict` — the auto mode classifier's raw decision for this call - `permission_mode` — the permission source (classifier, explicit deny, allowlist, etc.) that produced the final outcome
Filter on `classifier_verdict` to find calls the classifier was unsure about. Join with `tool_name` and you can see which tools repeatedly hit the classifier — a signal that your auto mode threshold is tight relative to your actual usage pattern.
**v2.1.302 follow-up (October 16): `CLAUDE_CODE_AUTO_MODE_MODEL`**
A new env var pins the model used for client-side auto mode classification, independent of the session model:
``` CLAUDE_CODE_AUTO_MODE_MODEL=claude-haiku-5-5 ```
Default is Sonnet for external sessions. Setting this to Haiku on a batch Workflow run reduces classifier overhead when the tasks are straightforward and the classifier rarely needs to deliberate.
**Known regression in v2.1.301 (fixed in v2.1.302):** `classifier_category` was dropped from `tool_decision` events in 2.1.301. Upgrade to 2.1.302 before building dashboards that read that field.
**Limits:** As of October 16, the official auto-mode docs page does not yet list `classifier_verdict` or `permission_mode`. The field names come from the Classmethod write-up and release notes — confirmed by implementation, not yet official reference. Server-side auto mode decisions are not emitted through client OTel, so this only covers client-side classifier decisions.
**Sources:** [Claude Code v2.1.301 OTel changes — dev.classmethod.jp](https://dev.classmethod.jp/en/articles/20261016-cc-updates-v2-1-301/) · [Claude Code telemetry with OpenTelemetry — openobserve.ai](https://openobserve.ai/blog/claude-agent-sdk-observability-opentelemetry/) · [Claude Code auto mode config — code.claude.com](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/auto-mode-config.md)

item.title: You're Regenerating in Claude Design for Changes That Belong in Your Editor — Here Is the Decision Rule for When to Stay vs. When to Switch to Claude Code
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: Use Claude Design for structural and aesthetic changes; switch to Claude Code once the design is settled. Inline canvas adjustments handle small visual nudges without burning a generation.
item.content:encoded:
**Use Claude Design for layout overhauls and aesthetic direction; switch to Claude Code the moment you're adjusting an implementation detail — spacing values, component props, a media query. Inline canvas adjustments handle small visual nudges without spending a generation.**
**What you'll be able to do after this:** Decide in under 30 seconds which tool a UI change belongs in, and stop re-exporting a design after you've already iterated in code.
**Three takeaways:**
1. **Structural and aesthetic changes → Claude Design.** A new section, a layout overhaul, a color direction shift, a different typographic treatment — these require the model to understand overall design intent. Give them to Claude Design via chat, where it can reason about the whole composition.
2. **Implementation changes → Claude Code.** Spacing values, responsive breakpoints, a component prop, a CSS custom property, a WCAG fix — these live in code, don't require design intent, and won't sync back to the canvas anyway. Fix them in your editor; a round-trip through Claude Design costs a full generation and returns the same structure with a slightly different implementation.
3. **Small visual nudges → inline adjustments first.** Claude Design's inline canvas comments let you adjust targeted properties without triggering a full generation. Use them for minor visual tuning before deciding whether a change is substantial enough to warrant a chat prompt.
**Concrete walk-through:**
You have a hero section. The client wants a more editorial direction — bigger headline, no gradient overlay.
1. **That's structural → Claude Design.** Prompt: *"Make the hero editorial: headline at 2× current size, remove the gradient overlay, bleed the image edge-to-edge."* Claude Design regenerates the section.
2. **Export and hand off.** Claude Code builds the component from the bundle.
3. **The headline/subheadline gap is 24px but you want 32px.** Implementation detail → fix it in code (`gap-6` → `gap-8`, or adjust the design token). Do not go back to Claude Design for this.
4. **Client wants to explore three different header directions.** Structural → back to Claude Design. Ask for variants in separate chat turns; save the state between them.
5. **Breakpoint behavior at 768px is broken.** Responsive bug → fix in Claude Code.
**The handoff is one-directional by default.** Code changes don't sync back to the Claude Design canvas. If you re-export from Claude Design after iterating in code, your code-side changes are overwritten. Treat the export as your starting point; once the component is in the repo, it lives in Claude Code.
**Limit:** Full regeneration in Claude Design draws from your plan's shared usage pool alongside chat and Claude Code. On a project with many components, keep structural sessions focused on one section at a time — whole-design prompts consume more than targeted ones. As of October 2026, there is no selective regeneration of one section while others stay fixed; chat iterates the entire canvas.
**Sources:** [Using Claude Design for prototypes and UX — claude.com/resources](https://claude.com/resources/tutorials/using-claude-design-for-prototypes-and-ux) · [Iterative refinement loop in Claude Design — mindstudio.ai](https://www.mindstudio.ai/blog/iterative-refinement-loop-claude-design-multimodal)

item.title: Claude Code --print Returns Freeform Text by Default — Add --json-schema to Get Schema-Pinned Structured Output Your Pipeline Can Parse Without Regex
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: Add --json-schema to --output-format json and Claude Code's headless mode puts a schema-validated object in .structured_output — no text-parsing or regex needed in your CI script.
item.content:encoded:
**When Claude Code runs headless with `-p --output-format json`, the answer lands in `.result` as a prose string. Add `--json-schema` and it lands in `.structured_output` as a validated object your script can destructure directly.**
When you pipe Claude Code output to a CI script, the default JSON envelope looks like this:
```json { "result": "The PR introduces a breaking change in getUser...", "session_id": "...", "total_cost_usd": 0.003 } ```
That `.result` is a prose string — you end up regex-ing for "yes" or "no" or building a secondary parse step. `--json-schema` removes that entirely:
```bash SCHEMA='{"type":"object","properties":{"has_breaking_change":{"type":"boolean"},"reason":{"type":"string"}},"required":["has_breaking_change","reason"]}'
claude -p "Analyze this diff for breaking changes" \ --output-format json \ --json-schema "$SCHEMA" \ | jq '.structured_output' ```
Output:
```json {"has_breaking_change": true, "reason": "Changed return type of getUser from string to User object"} ```
The envelope still includes `session_id`, `total_cost_usd`, and `is_error` — pipe through `jq '.structured_output'` to extract just the structured result, or use the full envelope for spend tracking.
**Three things to know:**
- Pass the schema inline as a JSON string, or from a file: `--json-schema "$(cat schema.json)"`. - An invalid schema causes an immediate CLI exit with an error (v2.1.205+ improved reporting; earlier versions silently fell back to freeform text — worth pinning your CLI version in CI). - `format` keywords (e.g. `"format": "date"`) are accepted but treated as annotations, not enforced. Use `pattern` if you need validation.
**Limit:** An open bug reported July 2026 shows array-type fields serializing as XML text in some versions. If your schema has array properties, test carefully against your installed version before relying on it in production CI.
**Sources:** [Headless mode — Claude Code docs](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/headless) · [CLI usage — Anthropic docs](https://docs.anthropic.com/en/docs/claude-code/cli-usage) · [`--json-schema` invalid-schema behavior — Claude Code issues tracker](https://claudeissues.com/issue/75875-docs-json-schema-flag-docs-omit-v2-1-205-fix-for-invalid-schema-silent-fallback)

item.title: Your Open-Model Inference Needs No Always-On Server — Modal Deploys vLLM on H100s from a Single Python File and Scales to Zero
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: Modal wraps vLLM in a Python decorator, deploys it on cloud GPUs in one command, and scales the container to zero when idle — the OpenAI-compatible endpoint works with your existing client code.
item.content:encoded:
**Modal deploys vLLM on real GPUs from a single Python file, exposes an OpenAI-compatible HTTPS endpoint, and scales the container to zero when idle — you pay only for requests, not for a server sitting warm.**
**What you'll be able to do after this:** run any HuggingFace model (including a fine-tune you trained locally) on H100 or H200 GPUs behind an OpenAI-compatible API, with no Dockerfile, no Kubernetes, and no idle billing.
## Where Modal fits
Ollama, vLLM, and managed endpoints (Fireworks, Together AI) all expose OpenAI-compatible APIs. The choice is about where the model runs:
- **Ollama:** local GPU you own — fastest, no latency, no cost per request; requires hardware - **Fireworks / Together AI:** managed endpoints you call — lowest ops burden, highest ongoing cost at scale - **Modal + vLLM:** you define the runtime in Python, Modal provisions cloud GPUs, container idles down between requests — right for a specific open model (e.g. a fine-tuned Mistral from the QLoRA tutorial) when you don't want to operate a persistent server
## Walk-through
```bash pip install modal modal setup # opens browser for one-time auth ```
Create `vllm_server.py`:
```python import modal
app = modal.App("vllm-openai")
vllm_image = modal.Image.debian_slim().pip_install("vllm")
@app.cls( image=vllm_image, gpu="H100", scaledown_window=15 * 60, # container idles down after 15 min ) class VLLMServer: @modal.enter() def load(self): import subprocess, time self.proc = subprocess.Popen([ "python", "-m", "vllm.entrypoints.openai.api_server", "--model", "mistralai/Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3", "--port", "8000", ]) time.sleep(40) # wait for weights to load into GPU memory
@modal.web_server(8000) def serve(self): pass ```
Deploy:
```bash modal deploy vllm_server.py # Prints: https://your-workspace--vllm-openai-serve.modal.run ```
Point your existing OpenAI client at the endpoint — no other code changes:
```python from openai import OpenAI client = OpenAI( base_url="https://your-workspace--vllm-openai-serve.modal.run/v1", api_key="unused", # vLLM doesn't require auth by default ) resp = client.chat.completions.create( model="mistralai/Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3", messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Summarize this diff in 3 bullets."}], ) ```
During development, `modal serve vllm_server.py` gives you a hot-reload URL without committing to a persistent deployment.
## Limits
**Cold start:** after the container idles down, the first request waits 30–60 seconds while vLLM loads model weights into GPU memory. The Modal Volume caches weights across deploys, so subsequent starts are faster — but first-request latency is real. If you need sub-second P99, keep a minimum replica running (`min_containers=1`) and accept the idle cost.
**Cost:** H100 time runs roughly $3–4/hour at current Modal pricing. That's economical for bursty workloads; for sustained high-throughput production, a managed endpoint is cheaper. The free tier includes credits to experiment.
**Fine-tuned models:** a model you trained locally needs its weights available to Modal — store them in a Modal Volume or point to a private HuggingFace repo using a `modal.Secret` for `HF_TOKEN`.
The official Modal example uses Gemma on H200s as the production-grade reference — it's the canonical code to follow; the code above is a minimal illustration of the pattern.
**Sources:** [Run OpenAI-compatible LLM inference with Gemma and vLLM — Modal docs](https://modal.com/docs/examples/vllm_inference) · [How to deploy vLLM — Modal blog](https://modal.com/blog/how-to-deploy-vllm) · [Deploying the Magistral vLLM Server on Modal — KDnuggets](https://www.kdnuggets.com/deploying-the-magistral-vllm-server-on-modal) · [vLLM on Modal — vLLM deployment docs](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/v0.9.1/deployment/frameworks/modal.html)

item.title: The Claude Design Export Shows One Viewport — Add a Three-Line Responsive Brief to Your Claude Code Handoff Before It Starts Building
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: Claude Design exports a single desktop viewport with no breakpoints. Without a responsive brief in your handoff prompt, Claude Code uses generic media queries that won't match your design system. Three lines fix this.
item.content:encoded:
**Claude Design gives Claude Code a desktop frame — no breakpoints, no mobile layout, no spacing-scale hints. A three-line responsive brief in your handoff prompt closes that gap before the first line of code is written.**
**What you'll be able to do after this:** write a responsive brief that takes your Claude Design export from "desktop only" to "works at 375px, 768px, and 1280px" in a single Claude Code session, without regenerating the design.
## What Claude Design does not export
Claude Design produces a visual composition at one viewport — typically the desktop width you designed at. It exports: - Layout structure and component arrangement - Color tokens, typography, and spacing values used in the design - Component states (hover, active, disabled) if you specified them
It does not export: - Breakpoints or responsive rules - Mobile layout changes (stacked vs. side-by-side, hidden elements, reordered sections) - Touch target sizes - Any instruction about which elements collapse, reorder, or disappear at smaller widths
Claude Code has no way to infer these from a desktop frame. Left to its own heuristics, it will emit generic `max-width` breakpoints that have no relationship to your design system's scale.
## The three-line responsive brief
Add this block to your handoff prompt, immediately after pasting the exported design or describing the component:
``` Responsive rules: - ≤640px (mobile): stack all flex rows to column, 16px side gutters, minimum 44px touch targets - 641–1024px (tablet): two-column grid max, sidebar collapses to drawer if present - ≥1025px (desktop): match the exported layout exactly ```
Adjust the column rules to match your actual design decisions. The gutters and touch targets should stay consistent across projects — make them a reusable snippet.
**Where to put it:** - In `CLAUDE.md` under a "Responsive contract" heading if you want it applied to every Claude Code session in the repo - Inline in the handoff prompt for a one-off component
## One step before the handoff
Before exporting, resize the Claude Design canvas to 375px and review the result. Claude Design will attempt a mobile adaptation — it's often incomplete, but it surfaces the decisions you haven't made yet: does the hero image disappear? Does the nav collapse to a hamburger? Does the pricing table stack or scroll?
Make those decisions in the design before the handoff. The responsive brief only works if you've actually thought through the mobile layout — it's a communication format, not a substitute for design judgment.
**Limit:** The brief tells Claude Code your rules but doesn't give it your full design-system token file. If your system has specific breakpoint values (e.g., `--bp-md: 768px`), either pass the token file or name the variable in the brief: "use `--bp-md` for the 641px breakpoint."
**Sources:** [Claude Design documentation](https://support.claude.ai/hc/en-us/articles/get-started-with-claude-design), [responsive design patterns with Claude Code](https://www.anthropic.com/news/claude-responsive-design), [Claude Design to Claude Code handoff mechanics](https://claudefa.st/handoff-mechanics)

item.title: Your Multi-Agent Run Shows Hex IDs in the Fleet View — Pass `name:` to Every Agent Call and Use `n:` to Find Any Session Instantly
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: Unnamed Agent calls show as hex IDs in `claude agents`. A `name:` on every call plus the `n:` filter in the fleet view makes navigating ten or more parallel sessions practical.
item.content:encoded:
**When you launch parallel agents without a `name:`, the fleet view shows hex IDs you can't distinguish at a glance. A one-field addition to every Agent call turns a wall of identifiers into a navigable dashboard.**
**What you'll be able to do after this:** open the fleet view during a multi-agent run, find any specific agent by name in under two seconds using the `n:` filter, and know which convention to use for naming agents across different call patterns.
## Why the fleet view shows hex IDs
Every agent call spawns a session with a generated ID. The fleet view (`claude agents`, or ctrl+] on Mac) lists running sessions by that ID unless you provided a human-readable name. With five or more parallel agents, all running in background mode, hex IDs make it impossible to tell which session is reviewing auth, which is analyzing deps, and which is now stuck.
Unnamed sessions also make `SendMessage` error-prone — you're copying a hex string instead of typing a purposeful label.
## The `name:` field on Agent tool calls
Every Agent tool call accepts a `name:` parameter. It's optional in the schema but should be treated as required in practice:
``` Agent({ name: "review:auth", description: "Review the auth middleware for security issues", prompt: "...", run_in_background: true }) ```
**Naming convention that works across projects:** `purpose:target` - `review:auth`, `review:payments`, `review:api` - `analyze:deps`, `analyze:bundle`, `analyze:types` - `generate:tests`, `generate:docs`, `generate:fixtures` - `fix:lint`, `fix:types`
The colon separator makes the `n:` filter especially effective — `n:review` matches all review agents at once.
## The `label:` field in workflow scripts
If you're writing workflow scripts (via the Workflow tool), the equivalent is `label:` in the `opts` object passed to `agent()`:
```js agent("Review the auth module for security issues", { label: "review:auth", phase: "Review" }) ```
`label:` and `name:` appear identically in the fleet view.
## Using `n:` in the fleet view
Open `claude agents` during a run. Type `n:` followed by any substring of a session name to filter immediately:
- `n:review` — shows all review agents - `n:auth` — shows any agent whose name contains "auth" - `n:review:auth` — exact match
Press Enter on a result to attach to that session and read its output. Press Escape to return to the list and filter again.
**Limit:** Names must be unique within a run — if two agents share the same name, the `n:` filter returns both and you can't tell them apart. For agents that iterate (e.g., multiple fix passes), append a suffix: `fix:types-1`, `fix:types-2`.
**Sources:** [Claude Code sub-agents documentation](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sub-agents), [Claude Code 2.1.287 release notes](https://www.havoptic.com/r/claude-code-2.1.287), [Claude Code workflow authoring guide](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/workflow-authoring)

item.title: Your Generated UI Passes the Prompt Test and Fails the Tab Key — Five Checks to Run Before the Claude Code Handoff
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: AI-generated UI reliably passes its own prompt but fails four checks a browser reveals: 375px squeeze, states audit, spacing scan, and the "AI look" test. Run these before handing off to Claude Code.
item.content:encoded:
**AI-generated UI almost always covers hover and skips focus-visible, breaks at 375px, mixes arbitrary spacing values, and has a hierarchy that treats every element equally — catch all four before the code lands in your repo.**
**What you'll be able to do after this:** run a systematic five-point review on any Claude Design output — or any AI-generated UI — in about ten minutes, and know whether to fix it with a prompt, fix it in your editor, or send it back for regeneration.
**Three things the automated tools already catch:**
The [axe-core/Playwright CI pass](https://cloudcodetree.com/ai-news/2026-10-11-01-axe-core-playwright-audit-ai-generated-ui-wcag-ci) catches WCAG contrast failures and missing ARIA attributes. Your build lint catches syntax errors. These five checks are what survives both.
## The five checks
**1. The 375px squeeze test**
Drag your browser window to 375px wide, or open DevTools device mode and select any small phone preset. AI-generated layouts are almost always desktop-biased: flex containers overflow, font sizes don't scale, touch targets collapse to unusable sizes.
If it breaks here, the fix is almost always CSS — not a regeneration. Hand the component to Claude Code with: "Fix the layout so it works at 375px without horizontal scroll. Do not change the desktop layout."
**2. The states audit**
Press Tab through every focusable element on the page. For each button, link, and input, check: - **focus-visible**: is there a visible outline? Generated code covers `:hover` and almost never adds `:focus-visible`. - **disabled**: if the element has a disabled state in the design, does the generated code reflect it visually? - **loading/submitting**: forms especially — is there a loading state, or does the button just sit there while the request runs?
Fix these in your editor, not in Claude Design. They're additive CSS and a handful of conditional classes, not structural changes.
**3. The spacing scan**
Open the browser inspector and click through three or four sections. Look at the raw `padding`, `margin`, and `gap` values. AI-generated UI almost always mixes arbitrary numbers — 13px, 22px, 37px — instead of a consistent scale.
If your design system has spacing tokens, hand them to Claude Code: "Replace all inline spacing values in this component with these token values: 4/8/16/24/32px. If a value falls between two tokens, round down."
**4. The hierarchy check**
Stand back and ask: is the primary action the most visually prominent element on the page? Generated UI tends toward visual equality — every card, button, and label gets roughly the same weight. If your secondary CTA competes with the primary one, fix the button sizing and contrast before committing the code.
**5. The "AI look" test**
Ask: if you showed this to someone and said "AI made it," would they immediately believe you? Common tells: identical card grids with no visual variation, glassmorphism applied to every surface, icon-heavy navigation with thin labels, and copy that survived from the generation prompt ("Your compelling value proposition here").
For structural issues (card grid sameness, layout defaults), regenerate in Claude Design with tighter constraints about visual hierarchy and variation. For surviving placeholder copy, fix it in the editor — it's faster than a regeneration loop.
## When to regenerate vs. fix in your editor
Checks 1 and 2 are almost always editor fixes: you're adding CSS properties and conditional classes that weren't generated, not changing the design intent. Checks 3, 4, and 5 are judgment calls: if the spacing inconsistency is pervasive, or the hierarchy is structurally wrong across the page, regeneration with a tighter prompt is faster than patching dozens of values by hand. If it's isolated, fix it in the editor and move on.
**Limits:** this review catches what's visible in a browser. It does not catch logic bugs in generated JavaScript, data-binding issues, or API contract mismatches — those belong to your normal code review, not this pass.
**Sources:** [AI-generated UI review checklist — snapcode.com](https://snapcode-micro-saas-web-de-ia-que-convie.onrender.com/blog/ai-code-generation-review-checklist) · [Evaluating AI-generated UI designs — Turing](https://www.turing.com/case-study/evaluating-ai-generated-ui-designs) · [Claude Code responsive audit — anthropic.com](https://www.anthropic.com/claude-explains/create-responsive-web-designs-efficiently-with-claude)

item.title: Your Pull Requests Can Now Get a Multi-Agent Review Pass Automatically — Claude Code Review Reaches GA for Team and Enterprise, Reviews Take 6-10 Minutes
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: Claude Code Review reached GA on Oct 15 for Team and Enterprise — reviews finish in 6-10 min per Anthropic, posts inline comments on logical bugs and security patterns. ZDR/HIPAA orgs excluded.
item.content:encoded:
**Claude Code Review is GA on Team and Enterprise as of Oct 15 — the multi-agent PR reviewer that reads your diff plus surrounding file context is fast enough for a normal merge workflow, per Anthropic's own report of 6-10 minutes per review.**
Claude Code Review is a separate feature from Claude Code itself. When a PR opens, it spawns a multi-agent session that reads the diff alongside the full context of the changed files, then posts inline comments on logical bugs, security patterns, documentation gaps, and test coverage holes. The multi-file context is the key difference from a diff-only linter: it can flag a bug introduced in one file because of an invariant defined in another.
## What changed at GA
Anthropic reports typical review time dropped from ~20 minutes in the research preview to 6-10 minutes. That's fast enough to sit in a normal PR merge workflow — you don't need to batch reviews or gate only on long-running PRs. Promotional review credits ($10,000 minimum) are available for eligible Enterprise organizations.
## Enabling it
Connect your GitHub organization in the Claude admin console (team.claude.com → Integrations → GitHub). Reviews fire automatically on new PRs once connected. Per-repo configuration allows you to set which branches trigger a review and which finding types are surfaced.
## What it finds
Multi-agent, specialized: one agent reads the PR, spawns focused sub-reviewers per concern area, then aggregates. During the research preview, Anthropic self-reported identifying over 500 vulnerabilities in open-source code. No independent comparison against Semgrep, CodeQL, or other SAST tools has been published, so treat that figure as directional rather than a benchmark.
## Limits to know before enabling
- **Not available for:** organizations with Zero Data Retention enabled, HIPAA configuration applied, or customer-managed encryption keys (CMEK). Check your org's compliance settings before announcing it to your team. - **Requires a Claude organization** even when developers reach Claude through AWS Bedrock, Google Cloud Vertex, or Microsoft Foundry — the review runs on Anthropic's infrastructure, not through the cloud provider's credential chain. - **Cost:** preview-era figures put reviews at roughly $15-25 each on token usage, scaling with PR size and complexity. Anthropic has not published GA-specific pricing, so verify current rates in the admin console before estimating costs. - **Not a test suite replacement:** Code Review reasons about intent and context, but it cannot run your tests or verify behavior. Treat its findings as a reviewer's suggestions, not a gate you fail blindly on.
**Why it matters:** the speed improvement is what actually changes the workflow. A 20-minute review sits outside the normal PR review loop; a 6-10 minute review fits inside it. If your team already uses Claude Code for the work, adding the automated review pass requires connecting GitHub once — the findings arrive in the PR alongside your human reviewers.
**Sources:** [Claude Code Review GA — Unite.ai](https://www.unite.ai/?p=486769) · [Claude Code Review blog post — anthropic](https://claude.com/blog/code-review) · [Code Review launch coverage — newsbytesapp.com](https://www.newsbytesapp.com/news/science/anthropic-launches-claude-code-review-for-teams-and-enterprise-users/tldr)

item.title: Your Unattended Claude Code Run Stops at the First 429 — `CLAUDE_CODE_RETRY_WATCHDOG` Retries Capacity Errors; Two Cap Variables Prevent Infinite Waits
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: CLAUDE_CODE_RETRY_WATCHDOG=1 retries 429 and 529 capacity errors automatically in unattended runs. Add CLAUDE_CODE_RETRY_WATCHDOG_MAX_WAIT_MS and the new MAX_USAGE_LIMIT_WAIT_MS (v2.1.301) to prevent indefinite blocking.
item.content:encoded:
**`CLAUDE_CODE_RETRY_WATCHDOG=1` retries 429 and 529 capacity errors automatically in unattended runs; pair it with two cap variables so a long outage or usage-limit reset doesn't hold your pipeline indefinitely.**
If you run Claude Code headlessly — nightly CI agents, overnight refactors, multi-step `--print` pipelines — a single 429 or 529 capacity error ends the run by default. The job exits cleanly, your workflow shows green, and the work was never done.
## The default without the watchdog
Claude Code retries transient errors with exponential backoff, up to `CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_RETRIES` attempts (default 10, hard-capped at 15 since v2.1.186). On a persistent capacity event, that retry envelope runs out in roughly 2.5 minutes before the process exits.
## Enable the watchdog
```bash CLAUDE_CODE_RETRY_WATCHDOG=1 ```
Set this in your environment, `.env`, or shell script. With it enabled, Claude Code retries 429 and 529 capacity errors indefinitely — no count limit — backing off up to 5 minutes between attempts. On v2.1.199+, it also retries server errors and timeouts with a ceiling of 300 attempts.
## Add the two cap variables
An infinite retry loop is correct for "provider is briefly overloaded." It is wrong for "the provider is down for three hours." Two environment variables give you control:
**`CLAUDE_CODE_RETRY_WATCHDOG_MAX_WAIT_MS`** — caps total time the watchdog will spend waiting across all retries. No default; unlimited without it. For an overnight run that must clean up by morning, `3600000` (one hour) is a reasonable ceiling.
**`CLAUDE_CODE_RETRY_WATCHDOG_MAX_USAGE_LIMIT_WAIT_MS`** — new in v2.1.301 (October 15): separately caps how long the watchdog blocks when the API response indicates a *usage-limit reset* rather than a capacity error. Without this, a usage-limit wait runs until the reset window closes (potentially hours) while your job window is open.
## One more backstop
Even with these caps, add a job-level timeout as a final guarantee. In GitHub Actions: `timeout-minutes: 90`. The env vars control Claude Code's internal retry logic; the job timeout is the OS-level guarantee that the runner reclaims its slot regardless.
## Putting it together
```bash CLAUDE_CODE_RETRY_WATCHDOG=1 \ CLAUDE_CODE_RETRY_WATCHDOG_MAX_WAIT_MS=3600000 \ CLAUDE_CODE_RETRY_WATCHDOG_MAX_USAGE_LIMIT_WAIT_MS=1800000 \ claude --print "your task here" ```
**One limit to know:** since v2.1.239, a 429 that carries a spend-limit or exhausted-credits flag fails immediately regardless of watchdog settings — that kind of limit won't lift until you take account action, so waiting forever is genuinely wrong. Log that exit code separately and alert on it; the watchdog won't mask it.
**Sources:** [Claude Code retry watchdog guide — developersdigest.tech](https://www.developersdigest.tech/blog/claude-code-retry-watchdog-unattended-runs) · [v2.1.301 MAX_USAGE_LIMIT_WAIT_MS — fyve.co.jp](https://fyve.co.jp/claude-code/articles/claude-code-retry-watchdog) · [MAX_RETRIES cap and watchdog docs gap — claudeissues.com](https://claudeissues.com/issue/70142-docs-error-and-env-var-docs-omit-claude-code-max-retries-cap-and-retry-watchdog)

item.title: Meta Releases Muse Spark Open: 816B-Param Open Weights for Coding Agents, Available on Fireworks AI and Groq
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: Meta released open weights for Muse Spark on October 15 — 816B-parameter MoE with 42B active per token, 1M-token context, built for coding and long-running agent workloads.
item.content:encoded:
**Meta released open weights for Muse Spark on October 15: 816B total params, 42B active per token (MoE), 1M-token context, built for coding and long-running agent workloads.**
Muse Spark has been a closed proprietary model since its April debut. The weights are now on Hugging Face and in the model catalogs of AWS, Google, and Microsoft. Seven inference providers launched on day one, including Groq and Fireworks AI — both are OpenAI-SDK-compatible, so routing calls to it is a `base_url` swap.
**License:** The Muse Model License is not Apache 2.0. Most developers can use it freely. Companies that sell hosted API *access to the model itself* and have cleared $20M in annual revenue need a separate agreement. Consumer products and applications built on top of it are not affected by the revenue threshold.
**Benchmarks (Meta's own harness):** 76.4 on Terminal-Bench 2.1 — behind Kimi K3's 85 on the same benchmark. 89.2 on MCP-Atlas (tool-use). Full independent evaluation results have not been published yet; treat the headline numbers as directional, not confirmed.
**What remains closed:** Meta's Muse Wonder series, which scores higher, is available only through Meta's own API and Muse Code. Muse Spark Open is the open-weight tier.
**Why it matters:** The first 816B open-weight model purpose-built for agentic coding. If your pipeline needs self-hostable, frontier-adjacent reasoning without a custom enterprise license, it's the first serious option at this scale. The Fireworks AI partnership means it's one config change away from an existing OpenAI-compatible inference setup.
**Sources:** [SiliconANGLE](https://siliconangle.com/?p=850737) · [The New Stack](https://thenewstack.io/meta-muse-spark-open/) · [Meta Muse Spark Open on Together AI](https://together.ai/blog/meta-muse-spark-open)

item.title: Reflection AI Releases Beam: 501B MoE, 23B Active Parameters, Apache 2.0 — and Nvidia Acquisition Talks
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: Reflection AI has shipped Beam, a 501B MoE open-weight model with 23B active parameters and an Apache 2.0 license — the first frontier-scale reasoning model open-sourced at this weight class. Weights dropped October 16. Nvidia acquisition talks are reportedly underway.
item.content:encoded:
**Reflection AI has released Beam — a 501-billion-parameter mixture-of-experts model with 23B active parameters, an Apache 2.0 license, and weights available on Hugging Face as of October 16.**
Beam is designed for reasoning-intensive workloads — coding, agentic pipelines, scientific reasoning, and mathematics — and is positioned as the first open-weight challenger to proprietary frontier reasoning models at this scale. With only 23B active parameters per token (MoE architecture activates one expert subset per forward pass), running Beam is within reach of a 4×A100-80GB or 2×H100 node — hardware many research labs and mid-size teams already have.
## Key specs
| | | |---|---| | Total parameters | 501B | | Active parameters per token | 23B (MoE) | | License | Apache 2.0 | | Weights released | October 16, 2026 | | Target workloads | Coding, agentic workflows, science, math | | Architecture | Mixture-of-Experts |
## Getting the weights
```bash pip install huggingface_hub
huggingface-cli download ReflectionAI/Beam --local-dir ./beam-weights ```
## Running with vLLM
```bash vllm serve ReflectionAI/Beam \ --tensor-parallel-size 4 \ --max-model-len 32768 \ --gpu-memory-utilization 0.95 ```
## Why Apache 2.0 matters
Most open-weight reasoning models use non-commercial or restricted licenses — Meta's Muse models use a custom commercial use agreement; some Mistral reasoning variants carry usage caps. Apache 2.0 means you can build and ship commercial products on Beam without negotiating an enterprise license, subject only to attribution.
For teams running self-hosted inference for privacy, cost, or compliance reasons, Beam is the first open alternative at frontier-comparable reasoning capability.
## Nvidia acquisition context
The Financial Times and Bloomberg have reported that Nvidia is in acquisition talks with Reflection AI. The company was founded by Matt Shumer and raised at a significant valuation earlier this year. No terms or timeline have been confirmed publicly.
**Practical takeaway:** If your pipeline runs coding agents or scientific reasoning workloads and requires a self-hostable model, Beam is the first serious open-weight option at frontier-comparable scale. The Apache 2.0 license makes it the only major open-weight contender suitable for commercial deployment at this capability tier.
Sources: [Let's Data Science](https://letsdatascience.com/news/reflection-introduces-beam-open-weight-reasoning-model-b6a0e32f), [VKTR](https://www.vktr.com/ai-platforms/reflection-ai-unveils-beam-a-501b-open-weight-model/)

item.title: Your RAG Pipeline Hits the Vector Store Even When Claude Already Knows the Answer — Adaptive RAG Classifies Each Query First and Routes It to the Right Source
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: Adaptive RAG adds one cheap LLM call before retrieval that classifies each query and routes it: skip the store for what the model already knows, hit your vectorstore for domain-specific questions, and fall back to web search for recency-sensitive ones. A LangGraph walkthrough.
item.content:encoded:
**Every query hitting your vector store adds latency and retrieval noise — Adaptive RAG inserts a lightweight classifier that routes each question to the right source before any embedding comparison runs.**
A standard RAG pipeline sends every query through retrieval. This works, but it wastes compute for questions the model can answer from its training data ("What is the capital of France?") and falls short for time-sensitive queries that need live data. [Adaptive RAG](https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.14403) (Jeong et al., 2024) adds one cheap LLM call — a query classifier — that routes to one of three paths: direct answer (no retrieval), vectorstore, or web search.
**What you'll be able to do after this:** skip retrieval for questions your model already knows, hit your vectorstore only for domain-specific content, and fall back to web search only when freshness matters.
## The three-way router
```python from langchain_core.prompts import ChatPromptTemplate from langchain_anthropic import ChatAnthropic from pydantic import BaseModel, Field from typing import Literal
class RouteDecision(BaseModel): source: Literal["vectorstore", "web_search", "direct"] = Field( description="Which knowledge source to use." )
llm = ChatAnthropic(model="claude-haiku-5-5") # cheap; single structured-output call structured_llm = llm.with_structured_output(RouteDecision)
ROUTE_PROMPT = ChatPromptTemplate.from_messages([ ("system", """Route the user question to the right knowledge source. - vectorstore: product docs, internal knowledge, domain-specific questions - web_search: recent events, new releases, time-sensitive information - direct: general factual questions, math, reasoning the model already knows
Return only the source name."""), ("human", "{question}"), ])
route_chain = ROUTE_PROMPT | structured_llm ```
## LangGraph state machine
```python from langgraph.graph import StateGraph, END from typing import TypedDict
class RAGState(TypedDict): question: str route: str | None context: list[str] answer: str | None
def classify(state: RAGState) -> RAGState: decision = route_chain.invoke({"question": state["question"]}) return {**state, "route": decision.source}
def retrieve_store(state: RAGState) -> RAGState: docs = vectorstore.similarity_search(state["question"], k=4) return {**state, "context": [d.page_content for d in docs]}
def search_web(state: RAGState) -> RAGState: results = tavily_client.search(state["question"])["results"] return {**state, "context": [r["content"] for r in results[:3]]}
def direct_answer(state: RAGState) -> RAGState: return {**state, "context": []} # skip retrieval; generate from weights
def generate(state: RAGState) -> RAGState: ctx = "\n\n".join(state["context"]) or "No retrieved context." prompt = f"Context:\n{ctx}\n\nQuestion: {state['question']}\n\nAnswer:" return {**state, "answer": ChatAnthropic(model="claude-sonnet-5-5").invoke(prompt).content}
graph = StateGraph(RAGState) graph.add_node("classify", classify) graph.add_node("vectorstore", retrieve_store) graph.add_node("web_search", search_web) graph.add_node("direct", direct_answer) graph.add_node("generate", generate)
graph.set_entry_point("classify") graph.add_conditional_edges("classify", lambda s: s["route"], { "vectorstore": "vectorstore", "web_search": "web_search", "direct": "direct", }) for node in ("vectorstore", "web_search", "direct"): graph.add_edge(node, "generate") graph.add_edge("generate", END)
adaptive_rag = graph.compile() ```
## Testing the routing
```python tests = [ ("What is the capital of France?", "direct"), # factual; no retrieval needed ("What changed in our API v3?", "vectorstore"), # domain knowledge ("Did Claude get updates this week?", "web_search"), # recency-sensitive ]
for question, expected_route in tests: result = adaptive_rag.invoke( {"question": question, "route": None, "context": [], "answer": None} ) print(f"{expected_route:12} → {result['route']:12} | {question}") ```
## Tuning the classifier
The system prompt is the only knob. Describe your domain in 1-2 sentences to distinguish "vectorstore" from "direct". Use `claude-haiku-5-5` for the classifier — it's a single 5-token structured-output call, costing less than $0.001 per query even at high volume.
For a complete walkthrough with relevance-grader nodes (checking document quality before generating), see the [LangGraph Adaptive RAG tutorial](https://langchain-ai.github.io/langgraph/tutorials/rag/langgraph_adaptive_rag/) and the [Mistral cookbook adaptation](https://docs.mistral.ai/resources/cookbooks/third_party-langchain-adaptive_rag_mistral).

item.title: Your Vector Store Doesn't Know What "Recent" Means — LangChain SelfQueryRetriever Parses Metadata Conditions From Natural Language Before the Embedding Search Runs
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: SelfQueryRetriever wraps any vector store and uses an LLM to pull structured metadata filters from natural language queries. Declare your filterable fields, install lark, and date ranges and category conditions become first-class retrieval parameters.
item.content:encoded:
**Your vector store treats every query as semantics — SelfQueryRetriever inserts an LLM parsing step that extracts metadata conditions from natural language and applies them as native store filters before the embedding comparison runs.**
When a user asks "find internal docs about authentication from 2026," a standard retriever embeds the full string and returns the top-k semantically similar chunks — ignoring "internal" and "2026" entirely, because those are metadata conditions the embedding has no way to express. [LangChain's `SelfQueryRetriever`](https://python.langchain.com/docs/integrations/retrievers/self_query/qdrant_self_query) closes this gap: an LLM reads the question, extracts structured filter conditions, and passes them to the vector store's native filter mechanism before the ANN search runs.
**What you'll be able to do after this:** route date ranges, category labels, access tiers, or any indexed payload field from natural language into the retrieval step without writing filter syntax by hand.
## Setup (Qdrant + LangChain)
```bash pip install langchain langchain-qdrant lark ```
```python from langchain_qdrant import QdrantVectorStore from langchain.retrievers.self_query.base import SelfQueryRetriever from langchain_core.structured_query import AttributeInfo from langchain_anthropic import ChatAnthropic
metadata_field_info = [ AttributeInfo( name="source", description="Document type: 'api-guide', 'changelog', or 'how-to'", type="string", ), AttributeInfo( name="year", description="Publication year as an integer", type="integer", ), AttributeInfo( name="tier", description="Access tier — 'public' or 'internal'", type="string", ), ]
llm = ChatAnthropic(model="claude-haiku-5-5") # cheap model; extraction only retriever = SelfQueryRetriever.from_llm( llm=llm, vectorstore=qdrant_store, document_contents="Technical documentation chunks", metadata_field_info=metadata_field_info, verbose=True, # logs the generated filter during dev enable_limit=True, # lets the LLM also set top-k from the query )
docs = retriever.invoke("internal API guides from 2026") # LLM generates: Filter(must=[FieldCondition(tier='internal'), # FieldCondition(year>=2026)]) # Qdrant applies this before the ANN scan — no pre-filter chunks reach scoring ```
## How the extraction works
LangChain sends the query and your field descriptions to the LLM, which returns a structured JSON query object. A `lark`-powered parser converts it to a `StructuredQuery`; a store-specific translator converts that into the vector store's native syntax — Qdrant `Filter`, Chroma `where` dict, Pinecone metadata filter. You write field descriptions once; the translator handles the rest.
## Limits
- **LLM mis-extraction** on ambiguous or multi-condition queries: inspect the generated filter with `verbose=True` during development. - **Range filters require indexed payload fields** in Qdrant — call `create_payload_index()` on each field you intend to range-filter; an unindexed range falls back to a full scan and can time out on large collections. - **Extra latency:** one additional LLM call per query, roughly 100–300 ms and a small token cost. - **`lark` parse errors on malformed LLM output:** wrap the invoke in a try/except and fall back to plain similarity search in production.
**Sources:** [LangChain SelfQueryRetriever with Qdrant — python.langchain.com](https://python.langchain.com/docs/integrations/retrievers/self_query/qdrant_self_query) · [Self-querying retrievers explained — elastic.co/search-labs](https://www.elastic.co/search-labs/blog/self-querying-retrievers) · [Qdrant payload filtering — qdrant.tech](https://qdrant.tech/documentation/search-patterns/vector-search-filtering/)

item.title: A Skill Is Not a Slash Command — It Loads Its Full Body Only When Invoked and Can Be Triggered Automatically When Claude Recognizes the Task
item.dc:creator: Chris Harper
item.description: Skills in .claude/skills/ keep their full body out of context until triggered — either by a slash command or automatically when Claude recognizes the task matches the skill's description. Only the one-line description is always loaded.
item.content:encoded:
**Skills (`.claude/skills/<name>/SKILL.md`) keep their full body out of context until triggered — by a slash command or automatically when Claude's task matches the description. A deploy skill that never fires today costs zero tokens today.**
You have probably used `.claude/commands/` for slash commands. A Skill is the richer version: it supports frontmatter for tool policies, model preferences, and a one-line description that Claude reads at session start to decide whether the task at hand matches.
## The two-part loading model
1. **Always in context:** the `description:` frontmatter field — one line, loaded at session start 2. **On trigger only:** the full SKILL.md body — loaded when you run `/<name>` explicitly, or when Claude identifies the current task as matching the description and loads it automatically
A skill that is never triggered today consumes nothing beyond its description line.
## Setup
``` .claude/skills/deploy/SKILL.md --- description: Deploy the app to staging, run smoke tests, and report pass/fail. allowed_tools: Bash, Read --- Run these steps in order: 1. `pnpm run build:staging` 2. `pnpm run deploy:staging` 3. `node scripts/smoke-test.mjs --origin https://beta.yoursite.com` Report each step's result and stop on first failure. ```
`claude /deploy` runs the exact workflow above. If you open a session and say "deploy to staging," Claude may load and run the skill without the slash command.
## When to use Skills vs. Commands
- **`.claude/commands/`** — a small prompt template with `$ARGUMENTS`; nothing fancy, always loads - **`.claude/skills/`** — a multi-step procedure with tool restrictions, optional frontmatter; loads only when invoked
Namespace subfolders with a colon: `.claude/skills/testing/generate-tests/SKILL.md` → `/testing:generate-tests`.
**Limit:** The `allowed_tools` / `disallowed_tools` frontmatter fields restrict what the skill can call, but exact syntax and support vary across versions — verify against [code.claude.com/docs/en/skills](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/skills) before building security-critical guards into skills. For hard security boundaries (blocking a destructive command), use a `PreToolUse` hook instead — those run before any tool call, not just skill-triggered ones.
**Sources:** [Steering Claude Code: skills, hooks, rules, subagents — claude.com/blog](https://claude.com/blog/steering-claude-code-skills-hooks-rules-subagents-and-more) · [Claude Code Skills vs Slash Commands vs Subagents — Towards AI](https://pub.towardsai.net/claude-code-skills-vs-slash-commands-vs-subagents-where-should-each-one-live-80bf1b846008) · [Stop Bloating CLAUDE.md: Where Workflows Actually Belong — Level Up Coding](https://levelup.gitconnected.com/stop-bloating-claude-md-where-your-claude-code-workflows-actually-belong-047112b85a02)

Check whether the evaluator had unilateral publication rights before treating their rating as independent validation.
